nameStory: The Atlantic deep-sea scallop gets its name from living in the deeper waters of the Atlantic Ocean, typically much farther offshore than most beachcombers ever venture. The "deep-sea" part distinguishes it from smaller, shallow-water scallops, though it was once called the "giant scallop" for its impressive size. When you see one washed up on a New England beach, you're looking at a traveler from the ocean depths!
description: The Atlantic deep-sea scallop is a large, fan-shaped bivalve mollusk with two hinged shells that can grow quite substantial in size. These commercially important shellfish live on the ocean floor in deeper Atlantic waters, using their powerful muscle to clap their shells together and propel themselves through the water when needed. Their shells are ribbed with distinctive radiating lines that fan out from the hinge, giving them their classic scallop appearance. You'll most likely encounter their empty shells washed up on beaches rather than living specimens, since they prefer deeper offshore waters.

idTips.label: Fan-shaped ribbed shells
idTips.description: The shell has distinct raised ribs that radiate out from the hinge point like the folds of a hand fan, creating a textured surface you can feel with your fingers

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably bigger than most scallop shells you'll find on beaches, with a substantial weight and presence when you pick one up

idTips.label: Circular to oval outline
idTips.description: Overall shell shape is roughly circular but often slightly taller than wide, with gently curved edges that feel smooth to trace with your finger

idTips.label: Wing-like projections
idTips.description: Small triangular flaps extend from either side of the hinge area, giving the shell a distinctive silhouette like tiny wings

idTips.label: Thick, solid shell
idTips.description: The shell feels heavy and substantial in your hand, much thicker and more robust than paper-thin shells of smaller scallops

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Shells range from creamy white to pinkish, orange, or brownish tones, often with subtle mottling or darker growth rings visible

habitat: These deep-water scallops live on sandy and muddy bottoms of the continental shelf in offshore Atlantic waters, typically in depths much too deep for casual diving or snorkeling. In New England waters, you'll find their empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, particularly along the outer Cape Cod shores and Maine's rocky coastlines where deep ocean currents can carry them inshore.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms, often appearing clean and well-preserved on beaches as wave action settles down.
seasonality.summer: Beach-washed shells become more weathered and bleached white by sun and sand, making the ribbed pattern still visible but less distinct.
seasonality.fall: Storm season brings new shells to shore, sometimes with other deep-water treasures like sea glass and unusual seaweeds.
seasonality.winter: Powerful winter storms are most likely to dislodge shells from deeper waters and carry them to New England beaches, though beachcombing conditions may be challenging.

funFact: Atlantic deep-sea scallops can actually swim by rapidly clapping their shells together like underwater castanets, jet-propelling themselves backwards through the water to escape predators like sea stars - making them one of the few bivalves that aren't just stuck in one spot!
confusionNotes: Smaller bay scallops have thinner, more delicate shells with finer ribs, while deep-sea scallop shells feel thick and heavy in comparison. Remember: "deep and thick" for deep-sea scallops versus "bay and thin" for bay scallops.
contextualKnowledge: This is the scallop you're eating when you order scallops at a restaurant - their large adductor muscle (the part that closes the shell) is prized as seafood. The shell itself has become an iconic symbol, famously used in the Shell Oil company logo and associated with pilgrimage routes in Europe.
compareHints: As the only Placopecten species in New England waters, compare it with bay scallops in the genus Argopecten, which are much smaller and have thinner, more fragile shells. Deep-sea scallops also lack the bright colors often seen in tropical scallop species, sticking to more muted earth tones.
